[MUQATIL:20:24-29/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Moses asks that his task of conveying the message to Pharaoh and his people be made easy rather than difficult.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p257#2/r3] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | God granted Moses’s requests; his speech impediment came from putting a coal in his mouth as a child after he pulled Pharaoh’s beard.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p257#2/r4] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | reports | Pharaoh meant to kill Moses, but his wife said the child did not understand and proposed testing him with a date and a coal; he chose the coal, causing the impediment.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p257#2/r5] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says Pharaoh called Moses an enemy after Moses took hold of his beard; Pharaoh’s wife proposed the test only to divert punishment from Moses.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · شاعر مجهول | reports | An unattributed poem depicts an echo in a desolate scene, distant in the dark of night, as an example of deceptive perception.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r10] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The Quran treats jinn as one of two accountable peoples, addresses them, calls them men, and indicates relations with humans. | mentions 72:6, 55:74
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r11] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | A group of jinn heard the Quran and returned to warn their people; the Quran also describes Satan's touch as causing madness, hence مس. | mentions 46:29, 2:275
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r12] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | reports | Ibn Qutayba cites sound reports from the Prophet and early Muslims about the unseen attendant and related beings.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r13] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | He allows that unusual events may occur in deserts, but says these incidents do not disprove realities people hear and see.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · شاعر مجهول | reports | A second unattributed verse says humanlike speech, once heard, proves too indistinct to understand clearly.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · الأخطل | reports | Al-Akhtal says a yearling fox in the desert looks like an armored horse when it climbs a rise, illustrating small things appearing large.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · النابغة | reports | Al-Nābigha says a herder carrying a load seems like a bird from his high, protected site, because height alters appearance.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · ابن أحمر | reports | Ibn Ahmar describes imagined shapes multiplying and a chameleon seeming to feed by pecking, as evidence of perceptual exaggeration.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r6] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | He likens professed belief paired with evasion to someone who pretends to take only morning drink while secretly gulping it down.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r7] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Belief in resurrection and the Prophet's report entails accepting barzakh torment; belief in divine questioning entails the angels' questioning in the grave.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r8] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | One who accepts Satan and jinn exist should also accept possession and their uncanny sounds or forms, as consistent implications of their existence.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p78/r9] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | rejects | He rejects calling Arabs universally ignorant or liars: scripture, prophets, earlier revelations, and peoples elsewhere corroborate what is reported.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p426/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · نافع | holds | Nāfiʿ opens the listed first-person yāʾs except ولي فيها and أخي اشدد, where he uses sukūn.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p426/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · أبو عمرو | holds | Abū ʿAmr uses sukūn on ولي فيها and حشرتني أعمى, opening the other listed first-person yāʾs.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p426/r3] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · ابن كثير | holds | Ibn Kathīr uses sukūn on ولي فيها، ويسر لي أمري، لذكري إن، على عيني إذ, and برأسي إني; he opens the rest.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p426/r4] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · حمزة، الكسائي، ابن عامر، عاصم عن أبي بكر | holds | These readers use sukūn on all listed first-person yāʾs.
[SULAMI:v1p441/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Ibn Ata asks to see none but God, act and speak only through knowledge of Him, and loosen the human knot of the tongue so that Moses speaks only what he has received from God.
[SULAMI:v1p441/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Ibn Ata asks God to uncover his heart so he sees none but Him, free him from self-regard, and make him speak only of God's favor and what brings him near.
[SULAMI:v1p441/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Ibn Ata reads the requests as opening the breast to hear God, easing the affair through abiding with Him, and loosening the ego's knot from the tongue.
[SULAMI:v1p441/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | Junayd says Moses asked God only for good character traits.
[SULAMI:v1p441/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · الحسين | reports | Al-Husayn reads the requests as progression into direct encounter: expanded capacity for confrontation, an eased course to God by God, and a loosened tongue; once granted, Moses sees only God's part in him and receives all he asked. | mentions 20:36
[THALABI:v6p243/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Moses asks that the task of delivering the message to Pharaoh be made easy for him.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p258/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Moses sought the means and preparation needed to convey the message, illustrating that an obligation presupposes ability to perform it.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p258/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Another account says Moses kept asking because he could hardly stop speaking with God and continued his prayers through the remaining questions.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p258/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Moses asks for an expanded breast and eased affair so he can bear hearing another's speech after hearing God's.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p388/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains the prayer as asking God to make easy the task for which Moses was sent.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:20:21-26/r8] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Moses asks God to make easy the task of conveying the message.
[JISHUMI:v6p4651/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Taysīr is making something easy, the opposite of making it difficult.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p271/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Moses asks God to ease the task of delivering the message to Pharaoh.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p62/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The initial general requests are then specified as chest and task; this general-to-particular restatement makes the plea more emphatic than a direct request alone.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p45#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · القاضي | reports | Al-Qadi says reciting the differing forms is permissible, provided they are transmitted from the Prophet.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p45#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو عبيد وغيره | reports | Many scholars, including Abu Ubayd, understand the seven letters as seven tribal languages, each contributing part of the Qur'anic language.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p45#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The proposed tribes are first Quraysh, then Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, where the Prophet was nursed and raised, followed by nearby tribes whose dialects he encountered around Mecca.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p45#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The author's list continues with Kinanah, Hudhayl, Thaqif, Khuza'a, Asad, Dabba and their associates, then Tamim, Qays, and related central Arabian tribes; these dialects constitute the seven letters' expressive variations.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p45#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ثابت بن قاسم | reports | Thabit ibn Qasim proposes seven groupings—Quraysh, Kinanah, Asad, Hudhayl, Tamim, Dabba and associates, and Qays—which together encompass the Mudar tribes and their dialects.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p45#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The author's account resembles Thabit's; these central Arabian dialects reached eloquence, remained free of foreign influence, and made the Qur'an's inimitability evident.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p45#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Their linguistic purity arose because they lived in central Arabia—Hijaz, Najd, and Tihama—where foreign peoples had not penetrated.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p46/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The Yemeni contribution, contrary to Abu Ubayd and al-Mubarrad's broader inclusion of Yemen, is limited to Yemeni words adopted by Hijaz Arabs; distinctive forms such as الزخيخ and القلوبي do not occur in the Qur'an.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p46/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Languages near Iraq were altered by Persian, Nabataean, and Hira Christian contact; northern Syria by Romans and Israelites; western mountain areas remained sparsely inhabited.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p46/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The intermediate tribes' language remained clear of foreign influence, and later philologists in Basra and Kufa recorded from them while avoiding Yemen, Iraq, and Syria.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p46/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Mecca, Medina, and Taif were also avoided as linguistic sources because foreign captives and traders had affected their speech; they had remained pure during the Prophet's time when contact was limited.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p46/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The seven letters are expressions from seven tribes: the same meaning may be conveyed in Qurayshi, Hudhayli, or another wording according to eloquence and concision; the Qur'anic word فطر was clarified to Ibn Abbas by a Bedouin's claim to have originated a well.

7 · author | holds | The request means: make easy for me the task for which You have commissioned me.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p28/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi resumes his earlier discussion of the benefits and conditions of supplication under 2:286 and adds points relevant to Moses’ prayer. | mentions 2:286
[RAZI-FULL:v22p28/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The highest degree of perfection is to be perfect in oneself and to perfect others; God is eternally perfect in Himself but perfects others in time.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p28/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although perfecting others is a perfection, its absence from eternity is no defect: perfecting means making something complete, and eternally making the already complete is impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p28/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The objection that God would lack a perfection if He did not perfect eternally fails because eternal action is impossible; impossibilities such as making a self or counting endless motions do not imply incapacity.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p28/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God brings some possibilities into existence because nonexistents are infinite; bringing all into being would mean an infinite number entered existence.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p28/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If God created all possibilities, He could create nothing afterward, since creating what already exists is impossible and this would turn ability into incapacity.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p28/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Creating everything would erase distinctions between the capable agent and what is naturally necessary; capacity is perfection, while natural necessity is deficiency.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p28/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection says the finite number of existent things is a small banquet compared with infinitely many deprived nonexistents; selection either presupposes an unexplained entitlement or is purposeless.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الله تعالى | reports | Razi cites a saying addressed to the intellect: through it God humiliates, rewards, and punishes; he uses this to frame reason as an honored gift, without giving a grading.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God grants reason, insight, and guidance; existence, life, power, and reason are four gifts, with reason completing the set.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | As the final Prophet is the best of the prophets and humans are the best bodily creatures, reason is best among the gifts because it comes last.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Reason’s innate necessary truths are like shining stars: just as stars guide travelers through earthly darkness, these truths guide minds toward the spiritual world.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Reason sees the mark of createdness on its own knowledge and gifts, inferring an inscriber from the inscriptions and recognizing that maker and building differ from what is made.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | No act occurs until the servant wills it, but a created will needs an agent; if the servant creates it, another will is needed endlessly, so God creates the will and truly facilitates affairs.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The objection is framed as God giving and withholding neither from stinginess nor generosity, which would seem unworthy of the Most Generous.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi answers that these doubts project human choices onto God; God is not questioned about what He does, while people are, as 21:23 states. | mentions 21:23
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The universal outpouring of existence from divine mercy is the general hospitality and comprehensive table meant by 7:156. | mentions 7:156
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Animals surpass inanimate things because they distinguish existence from nonexistence and use inanimate things as tools, whereas inanimates have no awareness of their own existence.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Just as mercy gave existence to some possibilities, it gives life to some existent things and leaves others inanimate; life is to inanimacy as light, sight, and existence are to their opposites.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Living beings perceive pleasure and pain, good and evil, and therefore need power to pursue what benefits them and flee harm; without it they would remain helpless prey.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p29/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Complete mercy grants power to some living beings, just as it grants life to some existent things and existence to some nonexistents.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p30/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Expanding the breast expresses the recipient’s readiness and facilitating the affair expresses the agent’s efficacy; God grants both, so the two prayers argue that all events occur by His decree, wisdom, and power.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p30/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One reading is that Moses asks not only for an open breast but also for the actual execution of his mission and attainment of its goal.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p30/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Another reading pairs God’s four gifts of existence, life, power, and reason with four services in prayer: standing, recitation, bowing, and prostration. | mentions 20:14
[RAZI-FULL:v22p30/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A further reading treats prophethood as a fifth gift and the prophetic mission as its corresponding service; Moses asks for help because of his weakness, limited means, and powerful opponent.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p30/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Supplication is a means of nearness to God, and Moses prayed here seeking that nearness; Razi says he will establish that prayer brings closeness and that Moses sought it.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p30/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi points to Qur’anic question-and-answer passages on theological matters: the crescents, the spirit, the mountains, and the Hour. | mentions 2:189, 17:85, 20:105, 79:42
[RAZI-FULL:v22p30/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | He also notes six successive legal questions in al-Baqara, beginning with what people should spend and the answer naming parents and relatives. | mentions 2:215
[RAZI-FULL:v22p41#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The soul receives unseen forms from the angelic realm through thought, then conveys them to the physical world through speech; thought is a great act of worship, and speech is its noble means of teaching others.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p41#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The requests form a sequence: chest expansion gives spiritual light, ease facilitates acquiring it, and the tongue then conveys that spiritual perfection to others.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p41/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أهل السنة | reports | The Sunnis explain Moses' request for ease as asking God to create ease in his affair.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p41/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Mu'tazilites interpret the request as God activating motives and incentives through facilitative acts of grace.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p41/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although God has already done every grace that could be done, some graces may only properly be given after this request; asking makes their provision fitting.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:24-30/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Moses requested aid in delivering the message through an expanded heart, an eased task, and release of his tongue's impediment.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:24-30/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Easing the task means facilitating the commanded work of conveying the message to Pharaoh.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:20:25-28/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Given the great mission, Moses asks for a heart able to bear its burdens, hardship, and revelation, and for God to ease it by creating means and removing obstacles.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:20:25-28/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The initial li leaves what should be expanded or eased implicit, then naming the breast and matter makes the request emphatic.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p53#6/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Make easy the task commanded of me: delivering the message to Pharaoh.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p53#6/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Make my affair easy reinforces expand my chest by repeating its meaning first generally and then specifically; naming chest and affair clarifies what is to be expanded and eased.
[QASHANI:20:25-28/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Making the affair easy means enabling the mission's audience to accept God's religion and supplying support against its opponents.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p326/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Knowing Pharaoh’s tyranny, Moses sought ease for a grave mission: acting as God’s vicegerent on earth and facing immense hardships.
[SAMIN-DURR:20:26/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The author distinguishes يسرته لكذا, as in 92:7, from يسرت له كذا, the construction used here. | mentions 9, 2, :, 7
[NASHR:v1p224/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Pronounce a moving yāʾ gently and lightly without turning it into hamza; give it its proper length when it is a madd letter, especially before another moving yāʾ.
[NASHR:v1p224/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | When yāʾ is geminated, preserve a single clear articulation instead of stretching it into a soft, chewed sound; excessive constriction is also an error.
[NASHR:v1p224/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Direct oral practice reveals the precise articulation, and repeated exercise brings it about.
[NASHR:v2p164/r7] NASHR, d. 833 · نافع وأبو عمرو وأبو جعفر | reports | These three open eight yāʾs: اجعل لي آية in Āl ʿImrān and Maryam, ضيفي أليس, both إني أراني forms, يأذن

[NASHR:v2p322/r8] NASHR, d. 833 · المدنيان وأبو عمرو | reports | The two Medinese and Abu Amr open the yāʾ in لذكري إن, ويسر لي أمري, على عيني, إذ تمشي برأسي, and إني. | mentions 20:14, 20:26, 20:39
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p16/r22] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Moses asks God to make his mission easy, clarifying the general request for an expanded heart.
[DURR-FULL:v5p564/r15] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · أسماء بنت عميس | reports | Asma bint Umays says she saw the Prophet at Mount Thabir praying with Moses' request for an expanded breast, ease, clear speech, and Aaron as support so they could worship and remember God abundantly.
[ITQAN:v3p192#3/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Clarifying after an initial ambiguity can show a meaning in two forms, strengthen it by making it arrive after expectation, or increase the pleasure of knowledge after partial understanding.
[ITQAN:v3p192#3/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The prayer to ease the task reinforces the request because the context is a mission that signals coming hardships.
[BURSEVI:v5p291/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Moses asks God to ease the mission of conveying the message by creating the means and removing obstacles.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p181#4/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The request for ease is tied to the command to go to Pharaoh (20:24): Moses recognizes the immense mission and asks God to make him patient under its trials and to ease it by enabling its means and removing obstacles; the prayer expresses utter dependence on God.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p181#4/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some connect the request to all of God’s address from “I am your Lord” through this point: Moses seeks an expanded heart to grasp subtle knowledge and revelation, perform worship fully, and endure preaching’s hardships.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p181#4/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Another explanation says Moses faced difficult duties in receiving revelation, serving God, and ordering the lower world; he sought enough strength to manage both worlds, since attending to one can impede the other.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p181#4/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī also reads the command to Pharaoh as implying prophetic duties toward God and people; Moses senses all of them and asks for help to fulfill them perfectly, so the request need not be restricted to the earliest divine address.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p181#4/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · علماء الرسوم | reports | For the formal scholars, “chest” here means the heart, either because it perceives or because it is the means of perception.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p182/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The added لِي intensifies the request: first the object of opening or easing is left implicit, then صدرى and أمري specify it; without لِي the clause would be complete but less elaborated. The same applies to both requests.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p182/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some say لِي adds a stronger connection, as in “The reckoning of people has drawn near” (21:1); al-Ālūsī replies that this does not conflict with the preceding explanation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p182/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الانتصاف | reports | Al-Intiṣāf says لِي shows that the benefit of opening the chest returns to Moses, since God is unaffected by whether it exists; al-Ālūsī applies the same point to the request to ease his task.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p209/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Moses asks God for steadiness, courage, and eloquence, and for circumstances that will help him convey and persuade through proof.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p209/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Heart denotes the mind; Moses asks for removal of fear and other barriers to action, then for ease by clearing impediments around the task.
[TABATABAI:20:25-32/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | prefers | Moses does not ask God to reduce the mission or compromise its demands; he asks that the same difficult and serious task be made easy for him personally.
[TABATABAI:20:25-32/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The phrase لِي in this context implies personal specification: make easy the task entrusted to me, not make the task intrinsically easier.
[ASAD-NOTES:20:25/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Moses asks God to make his task easy.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p24/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Moses’ prayer shows that he felt the weight of prophetic leadership and asked God for help, unlike worldly leaders who crave status.
